extracted.intended_audience: IB Mathematics students (SL & HL) preparing their Math Internal Assessment (IA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for students writing the IB Mathematics Internal Assessment (Math IA) for Analysis & Approaches or Applications & Interpretation at SL or HL, covering the five assessment criteria, procedural requirements, common mistakes, and practical tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion A: Communication (+4)
rubrics_metrics.description: This criterion assesses the organization and coherence of the exploration. A well-organized exploration contains an introduction, has a rationale (which includes explaining why this topic was chosen), describes the aim of the exploration and has a conclusion. Coherent exploration is logically developed and easy to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear introduction with rationale explaining why you chose this topic; straightforward description of the project's aim and context; well-organized body with complete explanations and all equations shown; concise conclusion connecting processes to prove/reject hypothesis; proper citations for external data sources. Show all work and include all equations; include necessary data in main text and put non-essential data in appendix; conclusion should explain how processes connect to answer the research question, assess model reliability, and suggest future work. Be concise and ensure logical development; paragraphs can be results followed by discussion or combined 'results and discussion'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion B: Mathematical Presentation (+4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate use of mathematical language, notation, symbols, and terminology with multiple forms of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard and correct notations, symbols, and terminology and define key terms when introduced. Include diverse representations (diagrams, tables, charts, formulae, graphs) and demonstrate effective use of technology and graphing software. Enhance graphical representation: optimize space, scaling and formatting; be consistent in fonts/colors/scale; craft descriptive titles and captions; accurately label axes with units; avoid distortions or misleading visuals; integrate graphs into textual analysis. Key guidelines for equations: format clearly using alignment/spacing and standard conventions; ensure equations flow logically and support the argument; define variables and terminology; use equation editors for readable expressions. Common mistakes: rounding errors, neglect of significant figures, undefined terms, difficult-to-read charts, unclear axis labels, misuse of terms. Use technology appropriately and reflect on formatting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion C: Personal Engagement (+3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine interest and deep connection to the topic reflected throughout the exploration, demonstrating independent thinking and creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show authentic interest beyond generic statements; connect the investigation to personal experiences or profound interests; present mathematical ideas in your own terms and explore unfamiliar concepts; demonstrate initiative and creativity in methodology selection; prioritize depth over breadth and show robust understanding of foundational principles. Make the investigation your own (ask thought-provoking questions, choose a novel research question, adapt or develop methods) rather than merely reproducing others' work. Uniqueness is beneficial but engagement is shown by approach and connection, not only topic novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion D: Reflection (+3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical review, analysis, and evaluation of the exploration showing learning journey and growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine results and discuss different approaches considered; explain chosen methodology and the significance of results; link discussion back to initial goals to 'come full circle'; reflect on the learning journey, challenges faced, and evolved understanding; consider real-world applications and broader mathematical contexts. Reflection may be interspersed throughout the IA or concentrated in the conclusion (if concentrated, the reflection must be strong). Discuss strengths and weaknesses of methods and propose future work. Being critical of results (including failed experiments) can yield strong marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion E: Use of Mathematics (+6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics relevant to the topic, commensurate with course level, and demonstrating genuine understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mathematics at an appropriate difficulty level—relevant to the topic and commensurate with the student's syllabus level. SL: 'correct' math with occasional insignificant errors can earn full marks; HL: math must be 'precise' with no errors for maximum score and should demonstrate deeper understanding and sophistication. Avoid overcomplicating (using complex math unnecessarily) and avoid using mathematics you do not understand. Using technology is recommended but students must show they understand what they are doing. Sophistication may come from HL syllabus content or from using SL content in a genuinely sophisticated way understood by the student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative requirements and scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules for the Math IA and overall scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Math IA is mandatory for Mathematics Analysis & Approaches and Mathematics Applications & Interpretation (HL & SL); it counts for 20% of the overall score. The official guide states 6–12 pages are enough, though reports may go up to 20 pages (no penalty if rubric satisfied and writing is concise). Recommended work time: around 20+ hours (roughly 10–15 hours class/teacher meetings plus 10–15 individual hours). Total marks: 20 across 5 criteria (A–E). Final mark is achieved by adding criterion marks (no fractions/decimals; scores rounded down if necessary). Be concise: bibliography and appendices are typically excluded from the page recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent pitfalls students make when planning and writing the Math IA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly formulated research question: fail to state variables and mathematical methods, or be too broad/narrow. Vague aim statements (e.g., 'relationship between them' or 'building my understanding') that lack specificity. Superficial engagement: merely stating interest without demonstrating it through reasoning and methodology choices. Lack of critical reflection: only describing steps rather than analyzing strengths/weaknesses and alternatives. Mathematical errors: rounding errors, ignoring significant figures, unclear graph labels; HL requires precision. Time mismanagement: spending excessive time on IA at the expense of exams. Other practical mistakes: unclear formatting, overlong rambling reports that lose marks in Criterion A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data, sources, presentation and appendices
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for using data (primary and secondary), citing sources, and including raw data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internet data (secondary data) is permitted but must be critically evaluated (discuss source reliability under Criterion D) and cited. Raw or large datasets should be included in an Appendix; include sample calculations and summary tables in the main body so examiners can follow logic without excessive flipping. Cite data sources, images, and any formulas not in the standard syllabus using a standard format (e.g., MLA or APA). Evaluate secondary data and usually perform more complex analysis to justify not collecting primary data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic integrity, assistance and topic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and expectations around tutoring help, collaboration, and using the same topic across subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism is taken very seriously. Tutors may act as a 'critical friend'—they can discuss feasibility, teach concepts, and review drafts for clarity but must not perform calculations or write the text for the student. 'Double dipping' (using the same topic for Math IA and another subject's IA, e.g., Physics) is strictly not allowed; you may study the same physical object but must have a completely different research question, data and analysis. Students may change topics early if needed, but pivot quickly if the chosen topic proves infeasible.
